title: Top 10 Essential Verbs in English, Part 2 (CEFR A0–A1 / A2)
dek: Master the second 10 high-frequency verbs in English: do/make, speak/talk/say/tell, look/watch/see, listen/hear, must/have to/should, come/leave, take/give, ask/answer, wait, and live. Conjugation tables on COSYtools.

blocks.text: Welcome to Part 2 of our 2-part core verb series for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! (Read [Part 1](top-10-verbs-en.html) if you missed it). Here we cover 10 core action, perception, and modal verbs. All conjugation tables and verb forms are consultable on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).

Ten verbs are enough to ask, answer, wait, listen, come and leave, and get things done on day one. <mark class="hl-handwritten">They are also the verbs where English learners make the most predictable mistakes</mark>: do or make, say or tell, look or watch, come or leave. The good news is that the mistakes follow patterns, and patterns can be learned.
blocks.say: Ten verbs are enough to ask, answer, wait, listen, come and leave, and get things done on day one. They are also the verbs where English learners make the most predictable mistakes: do or make, say or tell, look or watch, come or leave. The good news is that the mistakes follow patterns, and patterns can be learned.

blocks.text: Read this article out loud. For each verb, start with the table and say the forms without looking. Then read the three sentences in the 'Say aloud' section, hide them, and repeat them from memory, changing one word to talk about your own life. Finish with the mistake card: it shows the sentence many beginners say, and the one to say instead. Speak first, live the rule second: it is faster and more natural.
blocks.say: Read this article out loud. For each verb, start with the table and say the forms without looking. Then read the three sentences in the 'Say aloud' section, hide them, and repeat them from memory, changing one word to talk about your own life. Finish with the mistake card: it shows the sentence many beginners say, and the one to say instead. Speak first, live the rule second: it is faster and more natural.

blocks.quote: A verb learned in a sentence is worth ten verbs learned in a list.
blocks.say: A verb learned in a sentence is worth ten verbs learned in a list.

rows: 'Look at this', 'Watch a movie', 'I see a bird'.
'look for', 'look forward to', 'watch out', 'see you soon'.
'I must go', 'We have to study', 'You should rest'.
'must be', 'have to leave', 'should know', 'don't have to'.
'Come here', 'He came home', 'The bus leaves at 8'.
'Wait for the bus', 'Can you wait a minute?'.
'I live in London', 'She lives with her family'.

items:
**1. Do / Make:** Activities, tasks and creation.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I do my homework' vs 'I make breakfast'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'do business', 'do research' | 'make progress', 'make a mistake'.

**2. Speak / Talk / Say / Tell:** Communication and speech.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I speak English', 'Let's talk', 'Say hello', 'Tell me'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'speak fluently', 'talk with', 'say yes', 'tell a story'.

**3. Look / Watch / See:** Vision and attention.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Look at this', 'Watch a movie', 'I see a bird'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'look for', 'look forward to', 'watch out', 'see you soon'.

**4. Listen / Hear:** Listening and perception.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Listen to music', 'Did you hear that?'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'listen carefully', 'hear from', 'glad to hear that'.

**5. Must / Have To / Should:** Necessity, obligation and advice.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I must study', 'We have to leave now', 'You should rest'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'must be', 'have to go', 'you should try'.

**6. Come / Leave:** Arrival and departure.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Come here', 'He came home late', 'The train leaves at noon'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'come in', 'come from', 'leave for', 'leave behind'.

**7. Take / Give:** Exchange and transfer.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Take a coat', 'Give me a hand'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'take care', 'take time', 'give up', 'give a hand'.

**8. Ask / Answer:** Questions and replies.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Ask a question', 'Answer the phone'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'ask for help', 'answer questions', 'ask a favour'.

**9. Wait:** Patience and time.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Wait for the bus', 'Can you wait a minute?'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'wait for', 'wait in line', 'can't wait'.

**10. Live:** Residence and lifestyle.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I live in London', 'She lives with her family'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'live abroad', 'live well', 'live together'.

blocks.text: The memory map: ten verbs, five functions
blocks.say: The memory map: ten verbs, five functions

blocks.text: Instead of learning ten verbs one after another, sort them by function. When you want to say something, first ask: <mark class="hl-handwritten">am I acting, communicating, perceiving, obliged, or exchanging?</mark> The verb comes almost by itself.
blocks.say: Instead of learning ten verbs one after another, sort them by function. When you want to say something, first ask: am I acting, communicating, perceiving, obliged, or exchanging? The verb comes almost by itself.

items: **Acting & making:** do / make. Activities, tasks, creation.
**Communicating:** speak / talk / say / tell, ask / answer. Languages, conversations, questions.
**Perceiving:** look / watch / see, listen / hear. Vision and hearing.
**Obligation & advice:** must / have to / should. Rules, necessity, recommendation.
**Movement & exchange:** come / leave, take / give. Arriving, departing, transferring.
**Life & patience:** live, wait. Home, dwelling, waiting.
blocks.say: Acting & making: do / make. Activities, tasks, creation. Communicating: speak / talk / say / tell, ask / answer. Languages, conversations, questions. Perceiving: look / watch / see, listen / hear. Vision and hearing. Obligation & advice: must / have to / should. Rules, necessity, recommendation. Movement & exchange: come / leave, take / give. Arriving, departing, transferring. Life & patience: live, wait. Home, dwelling, waiting.
The 10 Core Verbs in Depth (Part 2)
1. Do / Make

blocks.text: **Do** and **make** both translate as one verb in many languages, which is why they cause so many mistakes. A simple rule of thumb: **do** is for activities, tasks and work that already exist (homework, the dishes, a job). **Make** is for creating or producing something new (a meal, a plan, a mistake, a decision).
blocks.say: Do and make both translate as one verb in many languages, which is why they cause so many mistakes. A simple rule of thumb: do is for activities, tasks and work that already exist (homework, the dishes, a job). Make is for creating or producing something new (a meal, a plan, a mistake, a decision).

rows: We make dinner and do the dishes.

items: **Activities & chores:** 'do the shopping', 'do the laundry', 'do your best'.
**Creating & producing:** 'make a cake', 'make a call', 'make money'.
**Common phrases:** 'do business', 'do research' | 'make progress', 'make a mistake'.
blocks.say: Activities & chores: 'do the shopping', 'do the laundry', 'do your best'. Creating & producing: 'make a cake', 'make a call', 'make money'. Common phrases: 'do business', 'do research' | 'make progress', 'make a mistake'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: What do you do on Sundays?
blocks.gloss: In this question, 'do' appears twice: the helper and the main verb. The answer is an activity.
blocks.context: A classmate asks about your weekend.
blocks.say: What do you do on Sundays?

blocks.targetText: I make coffee every morning before work.
blocks.gloss: Make = you create something (coffee) that did not exist before.
blocks.context: You describe your morning routine.
blocks.say: I make coffee every morning before work.

blocks.targetText: Can you do me a favour? I need to make an appointment.
blocks.gloss: 'Do a favour' is fixed. 'Make an appointment' is also fixed.
blocks.context: You ask a friend for help.
blocks.say: Can you do me a favour? I need to make an appointment.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: What are you doing? B: I'm making lunch. Can you do the dishes later? A: Sure, no problem!
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: What are you doing? B: I'm making lunch. Can you do the dishes later? A: Sure, no problem!

blocks.title: Do or make
blocks.why: Your language probably uses one verb for both. English splits them, and the split is partly by habit, so you must learn the pairs together.
blocks.rule: A mistake, a decision, a plan, a noise, a choice and a phone call are all **made**. Homework, housework, an exam (to take) and a favour are **done**.
blocks.say: Do or make. Not quite: 'I did a mistake.' Say this instead: 'I made a mistake.' Your language probably uses one verb for both. English splits them, and the split is partly by habit, so you must learn the pairs together. A mistake, a decision, a plan, a noise, a choice and a phone call are all made. Homework, housework, an exam (to take) and a favour are done. I made a decision. She did her homework. We made a plan.

blocks.question: I need to ___ a phone call.
blocks.explanation: A phone call is 'made': 'I need to make a phone call.'
blocks.say: I need to ___ a phone call.
2. Speak / Talk / Say / Tell

blocks.text: Four verbs, one idea: communication. They are not interchangeable. **Speak** is about the language or a formal talk. **Talk** is a conversation. **Say** is about the exact words. **Tell** needs a person to receive the information.
blocks.say: Four verbs, one idea: communication. They are not interchangeable. Speak is about the language or a formal talk. Talk is a conversation. Say is about the exact words. Tell needs a person to receive the information.

items: **Languages & formal speech:** 'speak Italian', 'speak slowly'.
**Conversation:** 'talk about the weather', 'talk to a friend'.
**Common phrases:** 'speak fluently', 'talk with', 'say yes', 'tell a story'.
blocks.say: Languages & formal speech: 'speak Italian', 'speak slowly'. Conversation: 'talk about the weather', 'talk to a friend'. Common phrases: 'speak fluently', 'talk with', 'say yes', 'tell a story'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Do you speak French? – A little.
blocks.gloss: Speak + a language.
blocks.context: A stranger asks for help in the street.
blocks.say: Do you speak French? – A little.

blocks.targetText: Can we talk after class?
blocks.gloss: Talk = a conversation between people.
blocks.context: You ask your teacher for a minute.
blocks.say: Can we talk after class?

blocks.targetText: He said he was tired, so I told him to rest.
blocks.gloss: Say = the words. Tell = tell someone something.
blocks.context: You report what happened.
blocks.say: He said he was tired, so I told him to rest.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Can I talk to you for a minute? B: Of course. What do you want to say? A: Tell me honestly: do you speak Spanish?
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Can I talk to you for a minute? B: Of course. What do you want to say? A: Tell me honestly: do you speak Spanish?

blocks.title: Say or tell
blocks.why: In many languages the same verb works with or without a listener. English 'say' cannot be followed directly by a person.
blocks.rule: **Tell** + person + information. **Say** + words (and 'to' + person if needed): 'She said to me' is possible but rare.
blocks.say: Say or tell. Not quite: 'She said me the answer.' Say this instead: 'She told me the answer.' In many languages the same verb works with or without a listener. English 'say' cannot be followed directly by a person. Tell + person + information. Say + words (and 'to' + person if needed): 'She said to me' is possible but rare. He told me the news. She said hello. I told them to wait.

blocks.question: He ___ me a funny story.
blocks.explanation: After a person, we use tell: 'He told me a story.'
blocks.say: He ___ me a funny story.
3. Look / Watch / See

blocks.text: English separates three kinds of vision. **See** happens by itself. **Look** is deliberate and directed. **Watch** is following something that moves or changes over time.
blocks.say: English separates three kinds of vision. See happens by itself. Look is deliberate and directed. Watch is following something that moves or changes over time.

items: **Seeing:** 'I can't see without my glasses'.
**Looking:** 'Look at the board', 'Look! A rainbow!'.
**Common phrases:** 'look for', 'look forward to', 'watch out', 'see you soon'.
blocks.say: Seeing: 'I can't see without my glasses'. Looking: 'Look at the board', 'Look! A rainbow!'. Common phrases: 'look for', 'look forward to', 'watch out', 'see you soon'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Look at the blackboard, please.
blocks.gloss: Look needs 'at' before the object.
blocks.context: Your teacher is explaining a new word.
blocks.say: Look at the blackboard, please.

blocks.targetText: We watch a film every Friday night.
blocks.gloss: Watch = follow a moving image for a while.
blocks.context: You describe your weekend.
blocks.say: We watch a film every Friday night.

blocks.targetText: I can see the sea from my window.
blocks.gloss: See = it enters your sight without effort.
blocks.context: You describe your flat.
blocks.say: I can see the sea from my window.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Look! There's a cat on the roof. B: Where? I can't see it. A: Watch, it's going to jump! B: Oh, I see it now.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Look! There's a cat on the roof. B: Where? I can't see it. A: Watch, it's going to jump! B: Oh, I see it now.

blocks.title: Look at, not look
blocks.why: Many languages use a single verb with a direct object. English 'look' always needs a preposition.
blocks.rule: **Look at** = direct your eyes. **Look for** = search. **Look forward to** = wait with pleasure.
examples: We look forward to the holidays.
blocks.say: Look at, not look. Not quite: 'Look the picture.' Say this instead: 'Look at the picture.' Many languages use a single verb with a direct object. English 'look' always needs a preposition. Look at = direct your eyes. Look for = search. Look forward to = wait with pleasure. Look at me. I'm looking for my keys. We look forward to the holidays.

blocks.question: Can you ___ a bird in the tree?
blocks.explanation: 'Can you see...?' is the natural way to ask if something is visible.
blocks.say: Can you ___ a bird in the tree?
4. Listen / Hear

blocks.text: **Hear** is passive: the sound arrives, you did not choose it. **Listen** is active: you pay attention on purpose, and it needs **to** before the thing you listen to.
blocks.say: Hear is passive: the sound arrives, you did not choose it. Listen is active: you pay attention on purpose, and it needs to before the thing you listen to.

items: **Listening:** 'listen to the radio', 'listen to your teacher'.
**Hearing:** 'I hear the rain', 'I can't hear you'.
**Common phrases:** 'listen carefully', 'hear from', 'glad to hear that'.
blocks.say: Listening: 'listen to the radio', 'listen to your teacher'. Hearing: 'I hear the rain', 'I can't hear you'. Common phrases: 'listen carefully', 'hear from', 'glad to hear that'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Listen to this song, it's amazing!
blocks.gloss: Listen + to + object.
blocks.context: You share your favourite music with a friend.
blocks.say: Listen to this song, it's amazing!

blocks.targetText: I can't hear you. Can you speak louder?
blocks.gloss: Hear = the sound reaches your ears.
blocks.context: A bad phone line.
blocks.say: I can't hear you. Can you speak louder?

blocks.targetText: It was nice to hear from you!
blocks.gloss: Hear from = receive news from a person.
blocks.context: You answer an old friend's email.
blocks.say: It was nice to hear from you!

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you hear that noise? B: No, I wasn't listening. A: Listen carefully... there! B: Oh yes, I hear it now.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you hear that noise? B: No, I wasn't listening. A: Listen carefully... there! B: Oh yes, I hear it now.

blocks.title: Listen to
blocks.why: Your language may use the verb directly with the object. English needs a small word, and it is easy to forget when you speak fast.
blocks.rule: **Listen + to**. **Hear** needs no preposition. 'Listen' is deliberate, 'hear' is automatic.
blocks.say: Listen to. Not quite: 'I listen music every day.' Say this instead: 'I listen to music every day.' Your language may use the verb directly with the object. English needs a small word, and it is easy to forget when you speak fast. Listen + to. Hear needs no preposition. 'Listen' is deliberate, 'hear' is automatic. Listen to me. I hear a bird. They listen to the radio.

blocks.question: I like to ___ to music.
blocks.explanation: Listen to + object. 'Hear' does not take 'to'.
blocks.say: I like to ___ to music.

blocks.title: Listening in a noisy world
blocks.content: English speakers often say 'I'm all ears' to show they are listening closely, and 'I hear you' to mean 'I understand how you feel', even if they do not agree. When you answer on the phone, a short 'Right', 'I see' or 'Mm-hm' shows you are listening. Silence can sound as if you disconnected, so keep making small sounds. Politely ask people to repeat: 'Sorry, could you say that again?' is always welcome, and native speakers will often slow down for you.
blocks.say: Listening in a noisy world. English speakers often say 'I'm all ears' to show they are listening closely, and 'I hear you' to mean 'I understand how you feel', even if they do not agree. When you answer on the phone, a short 'Right', 'I see' or 'Mm-hm' shows you are listening. Silence can sound as if you disconnected, so keep making small sounds. Politely ask people to repeat: 'Sorry, could you say that again?' is always welcome, and native speakers will often slow down for you.
5. Must / Have To / Should

blocks.text: All three verbs express obligation or advice, with clear differences in strength. **Must** is strong personal obligation or written rule ('You must stop'). **Have to** is an outside requirement ('I have to work'). **Should** is friendly advice or recommendation ('You should sleep'). In the negative, **mustn't** means forbidden, while **don't have to** means not necessary.
blocks.say: All three verbs express obligation or advice, with clear differences in strength. Must is strong personal obligation or written rule. Have to is an outside requirement. Should is friendly advice or recommendation. In the negative, mustn't means forbidden, while don't have to means not necessary.

items: **Rules & duty:** 'You must wear a seatbelt', 'Citizens must follow the law'.
**Daily necessity:** 'I have to wake up at seven', 'Do you have to go now?'.
**Friendly advice:** 'You should drink more water', 'We should leave early'.
blocks.say: Rules and duty: 'You must wear a seatbelt'. Daily necessity: 'I have to wake up at seven'. Friendly advice: 'You should drink more water', 'We should leave early'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I have to get up early tomorrow.
blocks.gloss: Have to = an obligation from outside (work, school).
blocks.context: You explain why you can't stay out late.
blocks.say: I have to get up early tomorrow.

blocks.targetText: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
blocks.gloss: Mustn't = it is forbidden.
blocks.context: The teacher explains the rules.
blocks.say: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.

blocks.targetText: You look tired; you should go to bed early, but you don't have to finish the chores tonight.
blocks.gloss: Should = good advice. Don't have to = not necessary.
blocks.context: You invite a friend to dinner.
blocks.say: You look tired; you should go to bed early, but you don't have to finish the chores tonight.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: I have a bad headache. B: You should rest and drink water. A: But I have to finish this report! B: You mustn't push yourself too hard.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: I have a bad headache. B: You should rest and drink water. A: But I have to finish this report! B: You mustn't push yourself too hard.

blocks.title: Mustn't or don't have to
blocks.right: 'You don't have to pay, it's free.'
blocks.why: In many languages, a single negative covers both 'forbidden' and 'not necessary'. English separates them sharply.
blocks.rule: **Mustn't** = forbidden. **Don't have to** = not necessary. After both, the verb has no 'to': 'You must go', 'You have to go'.
blocks.say: Mustn't or don't have to. Not quite: 'You mustn't pay, it's free.' Say this instead: 'You don't have to pay, it's free.' In many languages, a single negative covers both 'forbidden' and 'not necessary'. English separates them sharply. Mustn't = forbidden. Don't have to = not necessary. After both, the verb has no 'to': 'You must go', 'You have to go'. You mustn't smoke here. You don't have to come. She doesn't have to cook.

blocks.question: Entry is free: you ___ buy a ticket.
blocks.explanation: It is not necessary, so 'don't have to'.
blocks.say: Entry is free: you ___ buy a ticket.
6. Come / Leave

blocks.text: **Come** and **leave** are the twin verbs of movement. **Come** means motion towards the speaker or towards a destination ('Come to my house'). **Leave** means departing from a place ('I leave home at eight') or leaving something behind ('Don't leave your umbrella'). Both are irregular: come, came, come; leave, left, left.
blocks.say: Come and leave are the twin verbs of movement. Come means motion towards the speaker or towards a destination. Leave means departing from a place or leaving something behind. Both are irregular: come, came, come; leave, left, left.

rows: She came to visit us yesterday.
The train leaves at nine sharp.

items: **Arrivals & invitations:** 'come in', 'come home', 'come from Spain'.
**Departures:** 'leave the house', 'leave early', 'leave for work'.
**Common phrases:** 'come back', 'come on', 'leave me alone', 'leave a message'.
blocks.say: Arrivals and invitations: 'come in', 'come home', 'come from Spain'. Departures: 'leave the house', 'leave early', 'leave for work'. Common phrases: 'come back', 'come on', 'leave me alone', 'leave a message'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Where do you come from? – I come from Italy.
blocks.gloss: Come from = origin or nationality.
blocks.context: Meeting someone new in class.
blocks.say: Where do you come from? – I come from Italy.

blocks.targetText: What time do you leave home in the morning?
blocks.gloss: Leave + place directly, no preposition.
blocks.context: Talking about daily routines.
blocks.say: What time do you leave home in the morning?

blocks.targetText: She came back late and left early the next morning.
blocks.gloss: Irregular past forms: came and left.
blocks.context: Describing a busy travel schedule.
blocks.say: She came back late and left early the next morning.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: When are you coming to visit? B: I can come on Saturday! A: What time do you leave your city? B: I leave at eight and arrive at ten.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: When are you coming to visit? B: I can come on Saturday! A: What time do you leave your city? B: I leave at eight and arrive at ten.

blocks.title: Leave from or leave
blocks.why: Many languages use a preposition of origin ('partir de'). English uses 'leave' directly with the place of departure.
blocks.rule: **Leave** + place (no 'from'): 'I leave work at 5'. Use **leave for** + destination: 'I leave for Paris'.
examples: We leave for the airport now.
blocks.say: Leave from or leave. Not quite: 'I leave from home at eight.' Say this instead: 'I leave home at eight.' Many languages use a preposition of origin. English uses 'leave' directly with the place of departure. Leave plus place, no 'from'. Use leave for plus destination. She left the office. We leave for the airport now. He leaves home early.

blocks.question: What time do you ___ home for school?
blocks.say: What time do you ___ home for school?

blocks.title: Saying goodbye and leaving politely
blocks.content: When leaving a gathering in English-speaking cultures, it is polite to give advance notice: 'I'm afraid I have to leave soon' or 'I should get going'. Slipping away without saying goodbye ('an Irish exit') can be considered informal, whereas thanking your host with 'Thank you for having me' leaves a warm impression.
blocks.say: Saying goodbye and leaving politely. When leaving a gathering in English-speaking cultures, it is polite to give advance notice: 'I'm afraid I have to leave soon' or 'I should get going'. Thanking your host with 'Thank you for having me' leaves a warm impression.
7. Take / Get / Give

blocks.text: **Take** and **give** are fundamental opposites of exchange. **Take** brings an object towards yourself or along with you ('Take an umbrella'). **Give** transfers something to another person ('Give him the keys'). Both have irregular forms: take, took, taken; give, gave, given.
blocks.say: Take and give are fundamental opposites of exchange. Take brings an object towards yourself or along with you. Give transfers something to another person. Both have irregular forms: take, took, taken; give, gave, given.

items: **Taking:** 'take a bus', 'take a photo', 'take a break', 'take time'.
**Giving:** 'give a present', 'give advice', 'give someone a call'.
**Common phrases:** 'take care', 'give up', 'take it easy', 'give a hand'.
blocks.say: Taking: 'take a bus', 'take a photo', 'take a break', 'take time'. Giving: 'give a present', 'give advice', 'give someone a call'. Common phrases: 'take care', 'give up', 'take it easy', 'give a hand'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I take the subway to work every morning.
blocks.gloss: Take + public transport.
blocks.context: Describing your daily commute.
blocks.say: I take the subway to work every morning.

blocks.targetText: Can you give me a hand with this heavy box?
blocks.gloss: Give someone a hand = help someone.
blocks.context: Asking for help moving furniture.
blocks.say: Can you give me a hand with this heavy box?

blocks.targetText: He took my advice and gave his friend a second chance.
blocks.gloss: Irregular past forms: took and gave.
blocks.context: Recounting a personal story.
blocks.say: He took my advice and gave his friend a second chance.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you take the keys? B: No, I gave them to Sarah. A: Please ask her to give them back to me.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you take the keys? B: No, I gave them to Sarah. A: Please ask her to give them back to me.

blocks.title: Give to me or give me
blocks.why: English prefers the double object order: give + person + thing. When using 'to', the object comes first: 'Give the salt to me'.
blocks.rule: **Give + person + thing** ('Give me the book') OR **give + thing + to + person** ('Give the book to me').
examples: She gave him a warm smile.
Give the ticket to the conductor.
blocks.say: Give to me or give me. Not quite: 'Give to me the salt, please.' Say this instead: 'Give me the salt, please.' English prefers give plus person plus thing. Give me your phone number. She gave him a warm smile.

blocks.question: Can you ___ me a glass of water?
blocks.explanation: Pattern: 'give + person + thing' -> 'give me a glass'.
blocks.say: Can you ___ me a glass of water?

blocks.title: Please, thank you and polite requests
blocks.content: English speakers say 'please' and 'thank you' far more often than learners expect: when ordering coffee, getting on a bus, or when someone passes you the salt. 'Could you give me...?' and 'Could I take a...?' are polite ways to ask for things in shops and cafés.
blocks.say: Please, thank you and polite requests. English speakers say 'please' and 'thank you' far more often than learners expect: when ordering coffee, getting on a bus, or when someone passes you the salt. 'Could you give me...?' is a polite way to ask for things in shops and cafés.
8. Ask / Answer

blocks.text: **Ask** and **answer** work in pairs: someone asks, someone answers. Ask is flexible: you ask a question, ask for something, or ask a person. Answer can be a verb or a noun.
blocks.say: Ask and answer work in pairs: someone asks, someone answers. Ask is flexible: you ask a question, ask for something, or ask a person. Answer can be a verb or a noun.

items: **Questions:** 'ask a question', 'ask the teacher'.
**Answers:** 'answer the phone', 'answer a letter'.
**Common phrases:** 'ask for help', 'answer questions', 'ask a favour'.
blocks.say: Questions: 'ask a question', 'ask the teacher'. Answers: 'answer the phone', 'answer a letter'. Common phrases: 'ask for help', 'answer questions', 'ask a favour'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Can I ask you a question?
blocks.gloss: Ask + person + question.
blocks.context: You interrupt politely in class.
blocks.say: Can I ask you a question?

blocks.targetText: Could you answer the phone, please?
blocks.gloss: Answer the phone: it is a transitive verb here, no preposition.
blocks.context: Your hands are full.
blocks.say: Could you answer the phone, please?

blocks.targetText: I asked for the bill, and the waiter answered quickly.
blocks.gloss: Ask for + thing.
blocks.context: You tell a story about a restaurant.
blocks.say: I asked for the bill, and the waiter answered quickly.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Excuse me, can I ask something? B: Sure, go ahead. A: Can you answer a question about the homework? B: Of course. Ask me!
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Excuse me, can I ask something? B: Sure, go ahead. A: Can you answer a question about the homework? B: Of course. Ask me!

blocks.title: Ask for, answer to
blocks.why: In many languages, 'answer' takes a preposition ('answer to'). In English, 'answer' is followed directly by the person or the question.
blocks.rule: **Answer** + object, no 'to'. **Ask for** + thing. **Ask** + person + question.
blocks.say: Ask for, answer to. Not quite: 'I answered to the teacher.' Say this instead: 'I answered the teacher.' In many languages, 'answer' takes a preposition ('answer to'). In English, 'answer' is followed directly by the person or the question. Answer + object, no 'to'. Ask for + thing. Ask + person + question. Answer the question. She asked for water. He asked me a question.

blocks.question: Please ___ the phone, I'm busy.
blocks.say: Please ___ the phone, I'm busy.

blocks.title: Asking politely
blocks.content: Direct questions can sound sharp in English. Add 'Could you...?', 'Would you mind...?' or begin with 'Excuse me' before a stranger. A 'no' is often softened: 'I'm afraid I can't', 'I'd love to, but...'. When someone asks 'How are you?', they usually expect a short answer ('Fine, thanks, and you?'), not a detailed one. Learning these small phrases helps you ask and answer in a way that feels natural to native speakers.
blocks.say: Asking politely. Direct questions can sound sharp in English. Add 'Could you...?', 'Would you mind...?' or begin with 'Excuse me' before a stranger. A 'no' is often softened: 'I'm afraid I can't', 'I'd love to, but...'. When someone asks 'How are you?', they usually expect a short answer ('Fine, thanks, and you?'), not a detailed one. Learning these small phrases helps you ask and answer in a way that feels natural to native speakers.
9. Wait

blocks.text: **Wait** is a short verb with a big grammar trap: it needs **for** before the thing or person you expect. It also joins many time phrases.
blocks.say: Wait is a short verb with a big grammar trap: it needs for before the thing or person you expect. It also joins many time phrases.

rows: How long do we have to wait?

items: **With people & things:** 'wait for the bus', 'wait for a friend'.
**Time:** 'wait a minute', 'wait for ten minutes'.
**Common phrases:** 'wait for', 'wait in line', 'can't wait'.
blocks.say: With people & things: 'wait for the bus', 'wait for a friend'. Time: 'wait a minute', 'wait for ten minutes'. Common phrases: 'wait for', 'wait in line', 'can't wait'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I'm waiting for the bus.
blocks.gloss: Wait + for + the thing you expect.
blocks.context: You are at a bus stop and you text a friend.
blocks.say: I'm waiting for the bus.

blocks.targetText: Can you wait a minute? I'll be right back.
blocks.gloss: Wait + time (no 'for' needed).
blocks.context: You answer the door while on the phone.
blocks.say: Can you wait a minute? I'll be right back.

blocks.targetText: I can't wait for the holidays!
blocks.gloss: Can't wait = you are very excited.
blocks.context: You talk about your plans.
blocks.say: I can't wait for the holidays!

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Are you waiting for someone? B: Yes, I'm waiting for my sister. A: How long have you been here? B: Ten minutes. I can't wait to see her!
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Are you waiting for someone? B: Yes, I'm waiting for my sister. A: How long have you been here? B: Ten minutes. I can't wait to see her!

blocks.title: Wait for
blocks.why: In many languages, 'wait' takes a direct object. English needs 'for'. Without it, the sentence feels unfinished.
blocks.rule: **Wait for** + person or thing. **Wait to** + verb. **Wait** alone or with time: 'Wait a minute.'
blocks.say: Wait for. Not quite: 'I wait my friend.' Say this instead: 'I wait for my friend.' In many languages, 'wait' takes a direct object. English needs 'for'. Without it, the sentence feels unfinished. Wait for + person or thing. Wait to + verb. Wait alone or with time: 'Wait a minute.' Wait for me! I'm waiting for an answer. We wait to start.

blocks.question: Please wait ___ me at the door.
blocks.explanation: Wait for + person: 'Please wait for me.'
blocks.say: Please wait ___ me at the door.

blocks.title: Queueing: a national art
blocks.content: In Britain, people queue patiently, in a straight line, and it is considered rude to jump the queue. Saying 'Sorry, I think I was next' politely works if someone cuts in front. In many English-speaking countries, 'wait your turn' is a basic rule of public life, in shops, buses and cafés. Learners can also use 'Excuse me, is this the end of the line?' to join a queue. 'Hold on' and 'Just a second' are friendly ways to ask for a little time.
blocks.say: Queueing: a national art. In Britain, people queue patiently, in a straight line, and it is considered rude to jump the queue. Saying 'Sorry, I think I was next' politely works if someone cuts in front. In many English-speaking countries, 'wait your turn' is a basic rule of public life, in shops, buses and cafés. Learners can also use 'Excuse me, is this the end of the line?' to join a queue. 'Hold on' and 'Just a second' are friendly ways to ask for a little time.
10. Live

blocks.text: **Live** talks about where you have your home and how you spend your life. Notice the pronunciation: the verb **live** rhymes with 'give', but the adjective **live** (a live show) rhymes with 'five'.
blocks.say: Live talks about where you have your home and how you spend your life. Notice the pronunciation: the verb live rhymes with 'give', but the adjective live (a live show) rhymes with 'five'.

rows: I'm living in Madrid this year.
I have lived here for two years.

items: **Place:** 'live in a city', 'live on Main Street', 'live at number 5'.
**Lifestyle:** 'live well', 'live a healthy life'.
**Common phrases:** 'live abroad', 'live well', 'live together'.
blocks.say: Place: 'live in a city', 'live on Main Street', 'live at number 5'. Lifestyle: 'live well', 'live a healthy life'. Common phrases: 'live abroad', 'live well', 'live together'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Where do you live? – I live in Lyon.
blocks.gloss: Live + in + city or country.
blocks.context: A new student asks you a question.
blocks.say: Where do you live? – I live in Lyon.

blocks.targetText: She lives with her parents and two cats.
blocks.gloss: Live with = share a home.
blocks.context: You describe a friend.
blocks.say: She lives with her parents and two cats.

blocks.targetText: I'd love to live abroad for a year.
blocks.gloss: Live abroad = in another country.
blocks.context: You talk about your dreams.
blocks.say: I'd love to live abroad for a year.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Where do you live? B: I live in Manchester, in a small flat. A: Do you live alone? B: No, I live with my brother.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Where do you live? B: I live in Manchester, in a small flat. A: Do you live alone? B: No, I live with my brother.

blocks.title: Present tense with live
blocks.why: Many languages use the present tense for situations that started in the past. English needs the present perfect with 'since' and 'for'.
blocks.rule: **Live** is a state: use the simple present for facts ('I live in Rome'). Use **have lived** with 'since' or 'for'.
examples: I have lived here for five years.
She has lived in Paris since May.
blocks.say: Present tense with live. Not quite: 'I am living here since 2020.' Say this instead: 'I have lived here since 2020.' Many languages use the present tense for situations that started in the past. English needs the present perfect with 'since' and 'for'. Live is a state: use the simple present for facts ('I live in Rome'). Use have lived with 'since' or 'for'. I have lived here for five years. She has lived in Paris since May. They live in Berlin.

blocks.question: We ___ in a small town.
blocks.explanation: With 'we', no -s: 'We live in a small town.'
blocks.say: We ___ in a small town.

blocks.text: Grammar & Structure for A0–A1 / A2 Learners

• **Simple Sentence Structures:** Focus on Subject + Verb + Object.
• **Auxiliaries & Modals:** Use 'can', 'must', and 'be going to' for simple daily intentions.
• **Conjugations:** Check full present, past, and future tense tables on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).

blocks.say: Your 5-minute speaking routine

blocks.text: Five minutes a day, out loud, beat an hour of silent reading on Sunday. Here is a simple plan to repeat for one week: <mark class="hl-handwritten">one minute per step, no more</mark>.
blocks.say: Five minutes a day, out loud, beat an hour of silent reading on Sunday. Here is a simple plan to repeat for one week: one minute per step, no more.

items: **Minute 1, warm-up:** say the present, past and participle of do/make, come/leave, and take/give without looking at the tables.
**Minute 2, three verbs, three sentences:** choose three verbs and say one true sentence about your life for each: 'I live...', 'I have to...', 'I wait for...'.
**Minute 3, mistake hunt:** reread one 'Not quite' card and say the correct sentence three times, changing the subject each time.
**Minute 4, mini-dialogue:** play both roles of a dialogue with 'Can I ask...?', 'Could you give me...?', 'Do you understand?', and record yourself on your phone.
**Minute 5, replay:** listen to the recording and pick one sentence to keep for tomorrow. Write it on a note near your desk.
